title: Government Health Spending Triples, Households' Out-of-Pocket Expenditure Share Falls Sharply: National Health Accounts 2023–24
subtitle:
India Makes Major Strides Towards Affordable Healthcare as Out-of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) Share Declines by 21.5 Percentage Points, from 64.2% in 2013-14 to 42.7% in 2023–24

Government Health Expenditure More Than Triples from ₹1.30 Lakh Crore in 2013–14 to ₹4.14 Lakh Crore in 2023–24, Reflecting Sustained Expansion of Public Investment in Healthcare Over a Decade

Per Capita Government Health Expenditure Rises from ₹1,042 in 2013-14 into ₹2,959 in 2023-24, Reflecting Increased Public Spending on Healthcare for Every Citizen

Social Security Expenditure on Health Nearly Doubles as a Share of Total Health Expenditure, rising from 6% in 2013-14 to 11% in 2023-24, Strengthening Financial Protection

Government Investment in Primary Healthcare reaches ₹1.53 Lakh Crore, Reinforcing the Focus on Affordable and Accessible Healthcare at the Grassroots

Ayushman Bharat, Free Drugs and Diagnostics, Jan Aushadhi and Other Flagship Initiatives Support India's Progress Towards Universal Health Coverage
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 NOV 2026 2:13PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India has registered substantial progress towards making healthcare more affordable and reducing the financial burden on households, with Government Health Expenditure tripling and the share of Out-of-Pocket Expenditure borne directly by families declining sharply over the past ten years.
The
National Health Accounts (NHA) Estimates for India 2023–24
, released by the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, highlight a significant transformation in India's healthcare financing landscape. Between 2013-14 and 2023–24, Government Health Expenditure increased from approximately ₹1.30 lakh crore to ₹4.14 lakh crore, while Out-of-Pocket Expenditure as a share of Total Health Expenditure declined from 64.2% to 42.7%.
The simultaneous increase in public healthcare financing and decline in the proportion of spending borne directly by households reflects India's progress towards a more accessible, affordable and financially protective healthcare system.
The findings also underscore the Government's sustained efforts, under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, to strengthen public healthcare, provide comprehensive primary healthcare, expand financial protection, improve access to essential medicines and diagnostics, and bring quality healthcare services closer to communities.
Households' Out-of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) Falls by 21.5 Percentage Points
One of the most significant findings of NHA 2023–24 is the substantial reduction in Out-of-Pocket Expenditure as a share of India's total healthcare spending.
OOPE declined from
64.2% in 2013-14 to 42.7% in 2023–24
, marking a reduction of 21.5 percentage points.
This represents an important structural shift in healthcare financing, with a substantially lower proportion of total healthcare expenditure being financed through direct payments by households.
The decline has continued in the latest year, with OOPE reducing from 43.4% in 2022–23 to 42.7% in 2023–24.
The sustained downward trend reflects the expanding role of government-supported healthcare services and financial protection mechanisms. Initiatives aimed at improving access to free and affordable treatment, medicines, diagnostics and hospital services are supporting efforts to reduce dependence on direct household spending.
Government Health Expenditure Triples, Reaching ₹4.14 Lakh Crore
India's public investment in healthcare has witnessed substantial expansion over the period.
Government Health Expenditure rose from
₹1,29,778 crore in 2013-14 to ₹4,14,196 crore in 2023–24
, representing a threefold increase.
Over the decade from 2013–14 to 2023–24, the Government’s share in Total Health Expenditure (THE) increased by nearly 52%, registering an increase of 14.9 percentage points.
This growing contribution signifies a major shift in the country's healthcare financing pattern, with public resources playing a considerably larger role in meeting healthcare expenditure.
The increase in Government Health Expenditure has been accompanied by a corresponding reduction in the share of household out-of-pocket payments, reinforcing the importance of sustained public investment in improving healthcare affordability.
Public Healthcare Spending Per Person Increases Nearly Threefold
The NHA estimates also point to a substantial increase in public healthcare expenditure on a per capita basis.
Per capita Government Health Expenditure increased from
₹1,042 in 2013-14 to ₹2,959 in 2023–24
, representing an increase of approximately 2.8 times.
This increase highlights the significantly higher level of government expenditure on healthcare per person and reflects the expansion of public healthcare financing over the years.
Primary Healthcare Receives Major Boost; Government Spending Reaches ₹1.53 Lakh Crore
Strengthening primary healthcare has remained a central priority of India's healthcare reforms.
The NHA 2023–24 estimates show that Government expenditure on primary healthcare reached approximately
₹1.53 lakh crore
, reflecting the substantial scale of public investment in essential and community-level healthcare services.
This investment is particularly significant in the context of the expansion of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, which are bringing comprehensive primary healthcare services closer to communities.
These facilities provide services relating to preventive and promotive healthcare, screening for non-communicable diseases, essential medicines, diagnostics and other primary healthcare interventions.
The emphasis on strengthening primary healthcare is helping build a more comprehensive healthcare system, with greater focus on early detection, disease prevention and accessible care at the grassroots.
Social Security Financing Strengthens; Share Rises to 11%
The NHA estimates also highlight substantial growth in social security financing for healthcare, an important component of financial protection.
Social Security Expenditure on Health increased from
6% of Total Health Expenditure in 2013-14 to 11% in 2023–24
, an increase of 5 percentage points.
This growing share reflects the expanding contribution of organised financial protection arrangements, including Government-financed health insurance schemes such as Ayushman Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY), State-specific health insurance schemes, social health insurance and medical expenditure for government employees.
The increase in social security financing is particularly significant as it strengthens mechanisms designed to protect individuals and families against financial risks associated with medical treatment.
Private Health Insurance Expenditure also increased from 3.4% of Total Health Expenditure in 2013-14 to 10.2% in 2023–24 which reflects deepening of health insurance penetration across the country. This coupled with the increase in GHE provides enhanced financial protection to the public at large.
Flagship Government Initiatives Expanding Access to Affordable Healthcare
India's progress in healthcare financing has been accompanied by a series of major initiatives aimed at making healthcare more accessible, affordable and inclusive.
The Free Drugs and Diagnostics Initiatives, Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme, Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana and Affordable Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment (AMRIT) pharmacies are supporting access to essential healthcare services, medicines and medical products at affordable costs.
Ayushman Arogya Mandirs are expanding comprehensive primary healthcare services closer to people's homes, while Ayushman Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana is strengthening financial protection for eligible beneficiaries through cashless hospitalisation benefits.
These efforts are complemented by pharmaceutical price regulation undertaken by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority.
Together, these initiatives reflect a comprehensive approach combining stronger public investment, affordable medical treatment, primary healthcare expansion and financial protection.
A Decade of Transformation in India's Healthcare Financing
The National Health Accounts 2023–24 estimates bring out an encouraging picture of India's changing healthcare financing landscape.
Compared with 2013-14, the country has witnessed threefold growth in Government Health Expenditure, a substantial increase in the Government's share of Total Health Expenditure, a sharp reduction in the share of direct household spending and significant expansion in social security financing.
The most important development is the changing balance between public and household contributions to healthcare expenditure. A larger share of total healthcare spending is now being financed through government resources, while a considerably smaller share is being borne directly by households.
These trends represent important progress towards Universal Health Coverage and demonstrate the Government's continued commitment to building an affordable, equitable and accessible healthcare system.
About National Health Accounts 2023–24
The National Health Accounts Estimates for India 2023–24 constitute the eleventh round of estimates prepared by the National Health Accounts Technical Secretariat (NHATS) at the National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
The estimates are prepared using the internationally recognised System of Health Accounts 2011 framework.
The NHA Estimates 2023–24 may be accessed at:
https://nhsrcindia.org/national-health-accounts-records

title: Akashvani Launches ‘AIR Rising Stars’ to Provide National Platform to Young Musical Talent

AIR Rising Stars to Promote Young Musical Artists Below 30 Years of Age as Part of Akashvani’s 90-Year Celebrations
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 NOV 2026 8:56PM by PIB Delhi
content:
In a major initiative to encourage young musical talent and carry forward India’s rich and diverse musical heritage, Akashvani is launching the inaugural season of the “AIR Rising Stars”, a nationwide series of special musical concerts exclusively by the young artists below 30 years of age. The first season of the concert series will be organised at 26 locations across the country from 17th November to 30th November 2026. These concerts will provide distinguished national platform to young and emerging musical artists to showcase their talent and connect with wider audiences.
The initiative is being undertaken as part of the celebrations marking 90 years of Akashvani and reflects its continued commitment to identifying, nurturing and promoting musical talent across generations. AIR Rising Stars seeks to carry this legacy forward by placing the spotlight on the next generation of performers.
Focus on Young Graded and Emerging Artists
The concerts will primarily feature young graded artists of Akashvani below 30 years of age, representing different genres and musical traditions. In cases where suitable graded young artists are not available in a particular category, deserving ungraded young artists may also be provided an opportunity, subject to the prescribed guidelines and selection by the concerned Akashvani Station.
The concerts will showcase the diversity of India’s musical heritage through Hindustani Classical Music (Vocal and Instrumental), Carnatic Classical Music (Vocal and Instrumental), Light and Folk Music, Western Music and other regional musical forms, as appropriate to the participating stations.
Nationwide Celebration at 26 Locations
The concerts will be organised by 26 participating Akashvani Stations at Shimla, Dehradun, Delhi, Lucknow, Varanasi, Jaipur, Jalandhar, Suratgarh, Hyderabad, Vijayawada, Dharwad, Bengaluru, Mysuru, Madurai, Thiruvananthapuram, Tiruchirappalli, Kolkata, Imphal, Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Sangli, Nagpur, Puducherry, Jammu, Guwahati and Rampur.
Each participating station will organise a musical concert at a suitable venue, featuring promising young artists from the respective region. Eminent personalities, music connoisseurs, youth icons, students and members of the public will also be invited to encourage the participating artists and make the initiative a nationwide celebration of young musical talent.
Multi-Platform Broadcast and Digital Outreach
A key feature of AIR Rising Stars: Season-1 will be its extensive multi-platform broadcast and digital outreach, taking the performances of young artists beyond the concert venues to audiences across the country.
The concerts will be broadcast through the network of Akashvani Stations and will also receive coverage on Doordarshan, on “Raagam” Youtube channel of Akashvani, youtube channels of 26 Akashvani Stations, “NewsOnAir” mobile app and Prasar Bharati’s “WAVES OTT” platform. This integrated broadcast strategy will provide participating artists wider visibility through radio, television and digital platforms.
Cash Prizes for Top Three Performances
To encourage young artists and promote wider digital engagement, cash prizes and certificates will be awarded to the three participating artists whose performances secure the highest number of views on YouTube by 15th January 2027.
First Prize: ₹20,000
Second Prize: ₹15,000
Third Prize: ₹10,000
This initiative will provide additional recognition to young performers and encourage them to reach out to wider audiences through digital platforms.
It may be noted that Akashvani has a long tradition of organising the Akashvani Sangeet Sammelan , which has successfully completed 67 editions. Akashvani Sangeet Sammelan provides an esteemed platform for renowned Top Grade and A Grade artists to showcase their musical excellence, whereas AIR Rising Stars is an exclusive initiative aimed at providing a dedicated platform to young graded artists, who otherwise have limited opportunities to perform in such prestigious concert platforms organised by Akashvani.
Through “AIR Rising Stars:”, Akashvani aims to create a distinctive national platform for the next generation of musicians while strengthening the connection between India’s enduring musical traditions and its youth. The initiative will further reinforce Akashvani’s longstanding role as a promoter of India’s rich cultural and musical heritage and a nurturing ground for emerging musical talent.

title: 57th IFFI Celebrates Cinematic Ties with Partner Country Russia Through an Evocative Four-Film Showcase
content:
Goa, 15 November 2026
Under the theme of "Stories Without Borders," the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), proudly spotlights Russia as its esteemed Partner Country. Scheduled to take place in Goa from 20th to 28th November 2026, the festival reinforces enduring Indo-Russian cultural diplomacy by presenting a specially curated four-film package that bridges contemporary Russian auteur sensibilities with a celebrated Soviet musical classic.
Bringing together emerging directorial voices alongside a masterwork of satirical operetta, the Partner Country Russia section reflects the emotional breadth, stylistic audacity, and thematic depth of Russian filmmaking. From intimate explorations of family fractures, societal alienation, and personal redemption to a buoyant, Shostakovich-scored satire on urban aspirations, the showcase will offer festival delegates and cinephiles an immersive journey into the human condition.
Anastasia Kuzina’s
Bo Bo
(98 min), making its India premiere at the 57th IFFI, is a poignant rural drama about identity, acceptance and prejudice. Through Nadia, a young girl facing mockery for her facial hemangioma, the film explores her search for self-expression through music, reminding us that true transformation lies not in changing appearances but in overcoming societal prejudice.
Sidney Lumet’s Birthday
Raul Geidarov’s
Sidney Lumet’s Birthday
(92 min), winner of the Grand Jury Prize at the Vyborg National Film Festival, makes its India Premiere at IFFI57. This heartfelt coming-of-age drama follows 17-year-old Dato as he navigates family tensions, abandonment and forgiveness, exploring the resilience needed to heal generational wounds.
New Home
Nikita Grushin’s New Home (101 min), set for its World Premiere at IFFI 2026, is a moving drama about second chances and redemption. Following seven years in prison, Anna struggles to rebuild her life with the help of social services and Roman’s support. Featuring powerful performances, the film explores the challenges of reintegration, healing and confronting the past to find a new beginning.
Cheryomushki
Herbert Rappaport’s
Cheryomushki
(91 min), making its India Premiere at IFFI, is a delightful musical satire set in post-war Moscow. Following four young couples dreaming of better homes, the film blends catchy melodies, lively choreography and humour to expose bureaucratic corruption while celebrating community spirit and solidarity.
Through this specially curated selection, IFFI 2026 reaffirms the enduring cultural ties between India and Russia, while offering audiences an opportunity to engage with the diversity and evolving expressions of Russian cinema. The four films, spanning different genres and generations of filmmaking, reflect cinema's ability to transcend geographical boundaries and foster mutual understanding through shared human experiences.
The 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), scheduled to be held in Goa from 20th to 28th November 2026, will bring together filmmakers, industry professionals and cinema enthusiasts from India and across the world under the theme
“Stories Without Borders.”
With a diverse line-up of Indian and international films, special country showcases, premieres, competitions and industry engagements, IFFI 2026 continues its tradition of celebrating cinematic excellence and promoting cross-cultural exchange through cinema.

WAVES Film Bazaar, one of the region's most significant platforms for cinematic exchange, collaboration and business opportunities, will celebrate its 20th edition from 20th-24th November, 2026, at Taj Cidade de Goa Horizon, Goa, alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI).

Its programmes support filmmakers at different stages of production through industry collaboration, mentorship, financing and distribution opportunities.

title: India to strengthen engagement with Italy based 'International Physics Centre', says Minister Dr Jitendra Singh
subtitle:
India and 'International Centre for Theoretical Physics' (ICTP) initiate ‘India- ICTP Co-operation Fund’ to institutionalise scientific collaboration and researcher mobility: Dr. Jitendra Singh

Letter of Intent signed between DST and ICTP to strengthen long-standing research partnership and create greater opportunities for Indian scientists, researchers and students
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 NOV 2026 3:59PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India and the "International Centre for Theoretical Physics" (ICTP) have taken a significant step towards institutionalising their longstanding scientific partnership with the initiation of the ‘India-ICTP Co-operation Fund’, aimed at strengthening the engagement and mobility of Indian researchers with the international research centre.
A Letter of Intent (LoI) was signed between the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and ICTP in this regard during the visit of Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, Dr. Jitendra Singh, to ICTP in Trieste, Italy. The LoI was exchanged from the Indian side by Dr Praveenkumar Somasundaram, Head of the International Cooperation in DST.
Welcoming the initiative, Dr. Jitendra Singh expressed the hope that the India-ICTP Co-operation Fund would give greater impact to the existing engagement between the two sides and benefit Indian researchers. He noted the importance of institutionalising the ongoing association to provide further impetus to scientific collaboration and researcher mobility.
The initiative builds upon India's longstanding partnership with ICTP, which has seen active participation by Indian scientists, researchers and students across multiple programmes. Through the proposed Co-operation Fund, DST and ICTP seek to provide a more structured framework for this existing engagement, with particular emphasis on creating further opportunities for Indian researchers.
ICTP is a leading global hub for advanced research, higher education and capacity-building in physics, mathematics and related fields. Its association with India extends across research collaboration, academic exchange, workshops and capacity-building activities involving several Indian institutions.
Institutions including the Department of Science and Technology (DST), CSIR, leading universities and IITs have collaborated with ICTP through joint research, workshops and exchange programmes. Indian researchers regularly benefit from ICTP's visiting fellowships, diploma programmes and postdoctoral opportunities, while ICTP experts frequently engage with India's scientific communities working in high-energy physics, astrophysics, climate modelling and computational science.
The initiation of the India-ICTP Co-operation Fund and the signing of the LoI mark an important step towards strengthening these existing avenues of engagement and advancing the researcher mobility component of the partnership.
The collaboration has contributed to strengthening global networks of scientific excellence, bringing together researchers and institutions and supporting fundamental discoveries as well as innovations with societal impact. The proposed initiative is expected to further enhance the impact of this engagement and benefit India's scientific research community.
Dr. Jitendra Singh's visit to ICTP, which included a welcome lunch and the initiation of the researcher mobility programme, formed part of his official visit to Italy from November 11 to 15, 2026.

title: At the Climate Summit, India Makes the Case for a Sunday Bike Ride
subtitle: At COP31 in Antalya, Fit India presented Sundays on Cycle, a weekly ride that has not missed a Sunday since December 2024, and invited every country to host one community ride in the next year.
ministry: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 NOV 2026 6:33PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Most of the talk at a United Nations climate summit is about energy, finance and technology. On Saturday afternoon, at the International Solar Alliance Pavilion at COP31, India’s Fit India Movement made a smaller argument: that the climate fight is also won on ordinary streets, one weekend ride at a time.
“A city can build a bicycle lane, but only if its citizens choose to ride on it,” Mayank Srivastava, deputy director general of the Sports Authority of India, told the audience. “Infrastructure alone does not change how people live.”
The hour-long session, “Sundays on Cycle: From a Weekly Ride to a Way of Life,” was held at the pavilion (D 610) on the summit’s Children, Youth, Education and Skills Day at COP31, the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. Launched by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on 29 August 2019, the  Fit India Movement reflects his vision of building a healthy, active, and prosperous India. The movement aims to make fitness an integral part of every Indian’s daily life by encouraging people to adopt healthy lifestyles, engage in regular physical activities, practise yoga, and participate in sports.
The Fit India Movement of the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports presented the ride as a working example of Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), India’s campaign for sustainable lifestyles, with a simple message: one pedal, one purpose, one healthier world.
Sundays on Cycle, a free community ride, has been held every Sunday since Dec. 22, 2024. “It has not missed a single Sunday,” Mr. Srivastava said. Participation has reached close to 3.7 million at more than 30,000 locations across India, he said, and on World Bicycle Day this year, held with cycling’s world governing body, the Union Cycliste Internationale, organisers planned for 100,000 riders and about 400,000 turned up.
“More than the numbers, people have begun to take cycling seriously,” he said. “They return Sunday after Sunday, and what began as a campaign is becoming a habit.”
He argued that timing matters for countries like India. Many cities in the Global South are still being built, he said, and most trips in them are short enough to cycle. “If cycling becomes a habit before car dependence takes hold, those emissions need never be produced,” he said. “Avoiding them now is far cheaper than removing them later.”
Lindita Xhaferi-Salihu, who leads sectors engagement for Global Climate Action at UN Climate Change, delivered the keynote. She described Fit India as “a great model that can be replicated everywhere,” and spoke about her husband, who arrived in a new country as an 18-year-old refugee and found a community through a local handball club. “A community is only a community if somebody brings it together,” she said. “We cannot talk about communities if we don’t have somebody like Fit India bringing together people who share the same purpose and can act collectively for the betterment of their societies.” Climate negotiations, she added, are so technical that it has been hard to bring people along, and sport can be the “connective tissue” that does it.
A short film on the ride’s journey followed. In it, Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya, India’s minister for youth affairs and sports, who launched Sundays on Cycle in December 2024, described cycling as “much more than exercise” and “a powerful medium to carry the Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s message of Fit India.” “Through initiatives like Fit India Sundays on Cycle,” he said, “we must take this passion to every household and every community.”
A panel moderated by Dr. Bhairavi Joshi, an adviser to Fit India, asked whether a weekend ride can change how cities are built.
Jim Walker of the Walk21 Foundation, who joined a Sundays on Cycle ride in Delhi last month, pointed to Bogotá, Colombia, where a similar street opening began about 50 years ago and now draws about 1.6 million people every Sunday onto 125 kilometres of car-free streets. “We get stuck in the habits of our cities,” he said.
Felipe A. Ramírez Buitrago, director of urban mobility at the WRI Ross Center for Sustainable Cities, said such events “teach with example.” Once people enjoy the streets, he said, cities can make the case for protected lanes and links to mass transit.
Gashaw Aberra of ITDP Africa said car-free days in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, had helped produce the country’s first non-motorised transport strategy, which sets targets for walkways and cycle tracks. “Instead of what can we learn from Africa, I would say, what can Africa learn from India,” he said.
Sanjay Seth, executive director of The Energy and Resources Institute, said walking and cycling should be counted in India’s climate commitments and in state and city plans, not treated only as awareness campaigns. “We need to make sure that we build safely; then behaviour will follow,” he said.
Asked for one action every city should take in the next 12 months, the panellists answered in a word or two: Maud De Vries, chief executive of BYCS, said “just do it”; others named infrastructure, community engagement and obstruction-free pathways.
Closing the session, Ms. Amarjyoti, executive director of Fit India, invited every nation, city and partner present to host at least one community-led “active morning” over the next 12 months and to share the experience through the One Planet Network. The Turkish Cycling Federation, she said, was the first partner to join. “A cycling culture is not built in a day,” she said. “It is built week after week by people who keep showing up.”
The organisers also released an impact report on the first 97 editions of the ride.
Ashish Khanna, director general of the International Solar Alliance, delivered a special address. He said the session had drawn the largest attendance the pavilion had seen, and urged sports facilities, from stadiums to gyms, to adopt solar power. “We are so proud that we could fit something related to sports and cycling in our agenda,” he said.
The ride’s 100th edition will be held across India on Nov. 29. Fit India said it would share a Sundays on Cycle toolkit to help other cities start their own rides, and invited people around the world to ride that day in their own communities.
Fit India also invited COP31 delegates to a special Sundays on Cycle ride in Antalya on Sunday, Nov. 15, held with the Turkish Cycling Federation (Türkiye Bisiklet Federasyonu) from Konyaaltı to the old town of Kaleiçi, carrying the Sunday ride from India’s neighbourhoods to the summit’s host city. In India, the ride’s 98th edition on the same day marked Children’s Day with cycling and Zumba.
“Ride together, change together,” Ms. Amarjyoti said.
This special edition of Sundays on Cycle at COP31 was held under the banner “India Pedals & The World Joins In!”, and was organised in partnership with the Turkish Cycling Federation in Antalya, Türkiye, on Sunday, November 15, 2026. The route saw cyclists begin the rally at Konyaaltı Caddesi and conclude at Işıklar.
About Fit India – Sundays on Cycle
Launched by Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya, Union Minister for Youth Affairs and Sports, in December 2024, Fit India – Sundays on Cycle is organised by the Sports Authority of India under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, in collaboration with the Cycling Federation of India, Navavrati Foundation, Fitspire, the Centre for Integrative Health, MY Bharat and other partners. Rides are held every Sunday in all States and Union Territories, including at SAI Regional Centres, National Centres of Excellence, SAI Training Centres, Khelo India State Centres of Excellence and Khelo India Centres.
The COP31 session was supported by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, the Sports Authority of India, Fit India, Mission LiFE, the International Solar Alliance and BYCS India Foundation.

Its crest symbolises energy and forward movement, while its eyes represent focus, intelligence and spirit. The beak signifies determination and leadership, and its blue and turquoise feathers convey vibrancy, freedom and confidence.

title: NITI Aayog to launch National Workshop Series drawing lessons for the nation from 25 years of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi as Head of Government
subtitle:
Five National Workshops on leadership, delivery, inclusion, civilisational identity and India’s global role, from November 2026 to October 2027

Accounts from Kutch, Covid-19, Lakhpati Didi and the Space Sector to open the series
date:

content:
NITI Aayog will launch a series of five National Workshops on 17 November 2026 to draw lessons from twenty-five years of the Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi, as Head of Government. The series will study this quarter century of public leadership so that its lessons become part of the nation’s shared knowledge. It will document the experiences of those who were part of this journey and translate them into knowledge that benefits all.
The Prime Minister assumed office as Chief Minister of Gujarat on 7 October 2001. After serving for more than twelve years in that office, he assumed office as Prime Minister of India in May 2014 and is now serving his third successive term. With the completion of twenty-five years on 7 October 2026, this marks the longest continuous tenure at the head of an elected government in India. Throughout this period, governance has been anchored in the idea of the Pradhan Sevak, under which every office of government exists to serve the citizens. Antyodaya has set the measure of progress at the last person. Jan Bhagidari has made development a people’s movement. The principle of Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas, Sabka Prayas has further strengthened this as a shared national undertaking. The goal of Viksit Bharat by 2047 has provided this approach a long horizon, asking every institution to plan and act for India as it approaches the centenary of Independence.
Much of what India has learnt about governing at this scale is held in the experience of the officers, institutions and citizens who took and carried through these decisions. The series will record their first-hand accounts and examine them with academic rigour. It will develop them into institutional learning material, including case studies, research papers and teaching material, for civil servants, training institutions, universities, students and the wider public.
The five National Workshops will be focus on the following governance themes: “Leadership as Mission” in November 2026, “Governance as Delivery” in January 2027, “Development as Inclusion” in April 2027, “Civilisational Identity” in July 2027 and “India as a Global Force” in September 2027.
The first National Workshop, “Leadership as Mission”, will be held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi on 17th November 2026. It will study leadership through the specific decisions in which it becomes visible and the manner in which those decisions are translated into outcomes for citizens. Shri Anurag Jain, Chief Executive Officer, NITI Aayog, will welcome the participants and Shri Ashok Kumar Lahiri, Vice Chairman, NITI Aayog, will deliver the opening remarks. Dr. P.K. Mishra, Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, will deliver the inaugural keynote address, and Shri Uday Kotak, Founder, Kotak Mahindra Bank, will deliver a keynote address. Dr. R. Balasubramaniam, Member, NITI Aayog, will set out the framework of the workshop.
Four first-hand accounts from those who were directly part of significant decisions will form the core of the day. Shri Rajeev Topno, Additional Chief Secretary, Government of Gujarat, will speak on the reconstruction of Kutch following the 2001 earthquake. Ms. Preeti Sudan, former Union Health Secretary and former Chairman, UPSC, will speak on the response to Covid-19. Shri Shailesh Kumar Singh, former Secretary, Ministry of Rural Development, will speak on Lakhpati Didi. Dr. S. Somanath, former Chairman, ISRO, will share his experience on the opening up of the space economy.
A panel discussion on “Leadership for Viksit Bharat” will be moderated by Shri B.V.R. Subrahmanyam, former Chief Executive Officer, NITI Aayog. The panellists will include Shri Arvind Kumar Sharma, Cabinet Minister for Urban Development and Energy, Government of Uttar Pradesh, Prof. Vishal Gupta, Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, Ms. Debjani Ghosh, Distinguished Fellow, NITI Aayog, and Ms. Narayani Bhatia, Joint Magistrate, Hardoi.
Dr. T.V. Somanathan, Cabinet Secretary, will close the workshop and launch the Karmayogi Sankalpa on the iGOT Karmayogi platform. Through the Sankalpa, civil servants across the country will commit to a specific change in their own leadership practice.
Around 900 participants are expected to attend the workshop, of whom
250

The participants will also include 25 students of leading institutions and universities, and 50 community partners and beneficiaries of national flagship schemes. The group discussions will be guided by 25 case facilitators trained under the Amrit Gyaan Kosh initiative of the Capacity Building Commission. The proceedings will be streamed on the iGOT Karmayogi platform.

The Lakhpati Didi Initiative promotes sustainable household incomes through women's entrepreneurship and diversified livelihoods. It is being implemented under the
DAY-NRLM, which leverages the SHG network to provide rural women with financial access, skills and market opportunities.
The initiative's implementation reflects a phased approach to policy planning, institutional strengthening and community mobilisation. As of June 2026, t
he initiative has enabled 3.76 crore Lakhpati Didis, with a target of six crore by March 2029.An independent assessment by IIM Ahmedabad reported a 61 percent rise in average monthly household income and a 61.7 percent increase in average monthly savings in Lakhpati Didi households.
From Subsistence to Sustainable Livelihoods
The Lakhpati Didi Initiative is a flagship effort to strengthen women's economic participation in rural India. It aims to improve household incomes through sustainable livelihood opportunities and enterprise development. The government announced this initiative on
15 August 2023
. It initially targeted
two crore women
from
Self-Help Group (SHG) households
. The target was subsequently increased to
three crore
in February 2024. The initiative aims to create
six crore
Lakhpati Didis by
March 2029
. This target was envisioned in February 2026.
A Lakhpati Didi is an SHG member whose household earns at least
₹
1 lakh annually
. The benchmark considers total household income rather than individual earnings. Income from eligible
farm
and
non-farm activities
contributes towards this target. It is
calculated after expenses
and should remain
sustainable
across agricultural seasons or business cycles.
The initiative builds on the institutional network of the
Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)
. It seeks to move rural women beyond subsistence-based activities. Its approach combines livelihood diversification, financial inclusion, skill development and enterprise support.
3.76 Crore Rural SHG Women Enabled as Lakhpati Didis
By June 2026,
3.76 crore
rural SHG women had been enabled as Lakhpati Didis and
5.70 crore
women were identified as Potential Lakhpati Didis.
An
independent evaluation
of the Lakhpati Didi initiative by IIM Ahmedabad, covering 6,531 respondents in 17 states and UTs, reported
improvements in household economic conditions
. Average monthly household income increased by
61 percent
, while average monthly savings increased by
61.7 percent
.
Institutional Foundation: DAY-NRLM and the SHG Network
The Lakhpati Didi Initiative operates through DAY-NRLM. The government launched DAY-NRLM in
June 2011
. It organises women from poor rural households into SHGs. These groups promote
regular savings
and
collective financial activities
. They also connect members with banks, credit, training and markets.
As of 12 November 2026, DAY-NRLM had mobilised approximately
10.13 crore
SHG members into
94.40
lakh
SHGs.
SHGs function through a wider institutional structure.
Village Organisations
and
Cluster Level Federations
strengthen this network. This institutional foundation provided the
delivery mechanism
for the Lakhpati Didi Initiative. It enabled the government to build upon existing community institutions rather than establish a separate structure.
Evolution and Expansion of the Initiative
The initiative evolved through a series of policy decisions and implementation measures. In
2021
, the government advised States to promote sustainable livelihoods and diversify farm and non-farm activities among SHG households. In
August 2023
, the government announced the target of
enabling two crore rural SHG women
as Lakhpati Didis. Recognising the need to strengthen community institutions for achieving this goal, the government conducted
structured training
for
community cadres
between November 2023 and March 2024. Approximately
5.5 lakh
persons received training, which comprised of 12 modules delivered over 15 hours.
In
February 2024
, the Interim Budget increased the
national target to three crore
Lakhpati Didis. The
Lakhpati Didi portal
was also launched during this period. In
May 2024
, the
Digital Aajeevika Register
began recording the livelihoods and income of each household. Under this process, women are identified as ‘Potential Lakhpati Didis’ on the
LokOS platform
. Trained
Community Resource Persons (CRPs)
prepare business plans for individual households. Households then receive coordinated support in areas such as skills, finance, assets and markets. The national and state missions monitor progress through the same register. By
August 2024
,
one crore women
had achieved Lakhpati Didi status.
Further digital interventions followed in
July 2025
, with the introduction of the
Didi Business Plan tool
and a
financial-literacy application
for CRPs. The reported achievement in creating Lakhpati Didis increased to
two crore women
in
August 2025
. By
December 2025
, the initiative had achieved its
three-crore target ahead of schedule
. Subsequently, in
February 2026
, the government revised the national target to s
ix crore Lakhpati Didis
by
March 2029
.
Identification and Implementation Framework
The initiative follows a
community-led
identification and implementation process. It provides equal opportunities to SHG members across social and economic categories. Potential Lakhpati Didis are identified through consultations.
Trained Community Resource Persons (CRPs)
facilitate this process. They assess household livelihoods and support women in identifying additional income opportunities. The implementation framework follows several stages:
Identification:
Potential beneficiaries are identified through the SHG network and LokOS platform.
Income Assessment:
Household livelihoods, income and expenditure details are recorded. The Digital Aajeevika Register provides a common monitoring framework.
Enterprise Planning:
CRPs prepare individual business plans. These plans are consolidated to identify common requirements and sectoral opportunities.
Implementation Support:
Women receive coordinated assistance over three years. This includes training, finance, livelihood assets and market access.
Monitoring:
National and State missions review progress through digital records. State missions also validate reported achievements.
This process connects household-level planning with institutional support. It also allows interventions to respond to local livelihood requirements.
Leadership in Action: From Strategic Planning to Implementation
The initiative's implementation reflects a
phased approach
to policy planning, institutional strengthening and community mobilisation.
The groundwork began on
21October 2021
, when the government issued an advisory to States. It encouraged sustainable diversified farm and non-farm livelihoods among SHG households under DAY-NRLM. On
29 December 2021
, the government requested States to establish
time-bound targets
.
Subsequently, a communication dated
10 June 2022
introduced a mobile application-based household income
survey
to provide an
evidence base
for identifying household income gaps and planning targeted interventions.
On
6 September 2023
, the government organised a National Conclave, in which State missions, development partners and line ministries participated. The government released a
Strategy Note on Enabling Two Crore Lakhpati SHG Didis
. The strategy adopted an institutional approach by leveraging the existing DAY-NRLM network. The design recognised
four critical considerations
. Additional credit needed to support viable livelihoods and repayment capacity. Household income required a consistent measurement framework. State capacities varied and required context-specific support. Community institutions also needed adequate training to prepare household-level plans. These considerations were presented to the Prime Minister on
10 October 2023
. The Ministry of Rural Development subsequently submitted a
detailed action plan
to the Prime Minister's Office. It issued
implementation action points
on
16 October 2023
.
Consultations with States also identified
12 priority livelihood sub-sectors
. These included bamboo, honey, goat rearing, poultry and tasar silk.
During
2024
, the initiative received
continued leadership attention
through national addresses and direct interactions. The Prime Minister referred to it during
Mann Ki Baat
and other national addresses. He also
interacted with SHG women
,
drone operators
and
entrepreneurs
. A
Performance Review Committee
meeting took place in
July 2024
. The government also organised
regional consultations
across Guwahati, Srinagar, Jaipur, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Raipur during 2024-25. These engagements facilitated interaction with State missions and enabled discussions on implementation progress.
In
January 2025
, a
Lakhpati Didi tableau
featured in the
Republic Day parade
on Kartavya Path. The government conducted refresher training during
February-March 2025
. In
March2025
, it initiated discussions with the
Agriculture, Animal Husbandry
and
MSME
departments. These discussions focused on
convergence
between their respective schemes. The government also introduced a learning portal and chatbot in
October 2025
.
The government also strengthened
data governance
during
2025-26
. It introduced checks to identify unusual income entries. State missions were asked to reconcile discrepancies and certify reported figures. This helped
strengthen the credibility of progress assessments
. In 2026, implementation support expanded further through digital and institutional interventions. An application for
individual enterprise loans
was introduced on
21 February 2026
. An
upgraded version of LokOS
followed in
May 2026.
Regional workshops were organised at Gaya and Pushkar. A review involving all States took place during the
Rashtriya Grameen Vikas Sammelan
on
28-29 June 2026
. On 29 June 2026, a platform for producer groups and enterprises and a public
Lakhpati Didi dashboard
were also launched.
Overall, the implementation approach demonstrates the
importance of leadership beyond target-setting
. The government combined evidence-based planning with institutional capacity building. It leveraged existing community networks and promoted interdepartmental convergence. Regular reviews, digital tools and data validation strengthened monitoring and accountability. This combination enabled a nationally coordinated initiative to function through decentralised, community-led institutions.
Building Women-Led Rural Prosperity
The Lakhpati Didi Initiative represents an approach to rural livelihood development centred on women. It combines existing community institutions with enterprise planning and financial support. Its focus extends beyond increasing household income. It also promotes diversified livelihoods, entrepreneurship and community leadership. By enabling women to become active economic contributors, the initiative seeks to strengthen rural households. It also creates pathways for broader rural economic development.

title: Opening Up India’s Space Economy
subtitle: Enabling Private Players Participation
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 NOV 2026 11:05AM by PIB Delhi
content:
India’s space journey began with a strong, government-led institutional base built around ISRO and the Department of Space. As capabilities matured, the Government adopted a more facilitative approach that kept public-sector leadership while encouraging private innovation, investment and entrepreneurship. Policy reforms opened the entire space value chain to Non-Government Entities, with IN-SPACe as the single-window interface between Govt. and private entities and NSIL as the commercial arm. The Indian Space Policy 2023 defined each institution’s role, while liberalised foreign investment rules, clear authorisation procedures and dedicated funding schemes supported start-ups. These steps are steadily building a collaborative, industry-led and globally competitive space ecosystem.
Where It All Began – From State-Led Foundations to Global Leadership
India's space journey has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past decade. It has evolved from pioneering scientific research into a globally competitive space programme. This progress reflects sustained national ambition, institutional vision and indigenous technological innovation. Today, India is advancing towards a more commercially dynamic space sector. Growing private-sector participation is further expanding its industrial and technological capabilities.
The foundations of this journey were laid through a strong institutional framework. The Indian
National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR)
was established in 1962. It functioned under the Department of Atomic Energy and spearheaded India's early space research initiatives. Subsequently, the
Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)
was established in August 1969, replacing INCOSPAR. In June 1972, the Government constituted the
Space Commission
and established the
Department of Space (DoS).
ISRO was brought under the DoS in September 1972.
As India's space capabilities matured, the Government recognised the need for broader institutional participation. This required moving beyond a predominantly government-led operational framework. Accordingly, the Government adopted a more facilitative and outcome-oriented approach to space-sector governance. This approach retained public-sector leadership while encouraging private innovation, investment and entrepreneurship.
A landmark step in this direction came on 24 June 2020. The
Union Cabinet approved reforms enabling greater private-sector participation in space activities
. These reforms marked a significant shift towards a collaborative public-private model. They also laid the foundation for a more competitive and commercially driven space sector. These reforms redefined the institutional framework governing India's space activities. They positioned the private sector as an active partner in advancing national capabilities, commercial opportunities and global competitiveness.
Key Indicators
Highlighting the Scale of India`s Space Sector Transformation
Growth of Space Economy:
India’s space economy was estimated at about US$9 billion in August 2026, against about US$8.4 billion (about 2% of the global space economy) in 2023
Start-up Growth:
Registered space start-ups increased from one in 2014 to approximately 440 in August 2026.
Private Investment:
Cumulative investment in Indian space start-ups increased from US$100.5 million in 2021–22 to US$618.5 million by 31 March 2026.
Commercial Launches:
ISRO launched 399 foreign satellites between 2014 and January 2026, compared with 35 between 1990 and 2014.
Foreign Direct Investment:
By mid-2026, the Government received 11 FDI proposals worth ₹1,745.40 crore for the space sector.
International Cooperation:
As on June 2026, India's global partnerships expanded to over 300 space cooperation agreements across 61 countries and five multilateral organisations.
Collaborative Governance: Marketization of India's Space Sector (2020-2026)
Recognising the potential of private enterprises to expand India's space capabilities and strengthen its position in the global space economy, the Government of India announced major space-sector reforms on
24 June 2020
. The expansion of India's space programme also brought an opportunity to tap the growing global commercial space market and scale up industrial participation.
Read More on India’s Space Capability
Cabinet Approval of Reforms and Constitution of IN-SPACe (June 2020–November 2022)
The reforms enabled
Non-Government Entities (NGEs)
to participate across the entire space value chain. Their role expanded beyond supplying components and providing services.
The cabinet approval also established the
Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe)
as an autonomous agency. It operates under the DoS and serves as a
single-window interface
for private enterprises for regulatory clearances. Its mandate includes promoting private participation, authorising and supervising space activities, and facilitating access to ISRO facilities, subject to safety considerations and operational priorities. Its mandate
also
covers mission safety, launch readiness, orbital and frequency coordination, spacecraft registration and security requirements.
NewSpace India Limited (NSIL)
was established in March 2019 as the commercial arm of the DoS. Its mandate was subsequently expanded to commercialise technologies developed using public funds. NSIL was also tasked with aggregating demand from government and other customers. It would further market and sell these technologies and services in domestic and international markets. Meanwhile, private-sector space activities continued to remain subject to applicable licensing, safety and security requirements.
Further strengthening this institutional framework, the
Indian Space Association (ISpA)
was launched in October 2021. It provides an industry platform for engaging with the Government and supporting the growth of India's space sector.
IN-SPACe and NSIL Delivered Measurable Outcomes
NSIL revenues increased from ₹321.77 crore in FY 2021-22 to over ₹3000 crore in FY 2024-25.
NSIL signed 118 technology transfer agreements covering 83 ISRO technologies.
As of 31 January 2026,
IN-SPACe
had facilitated 71 technology transfers to industry and startups.
By mid-2026, 113 authorisations had been granted by IN-SPACe
to 52 NGEs, of which 18 were start-ups.
Six Indian Non-Government Entities launched 18 satellites, while 25 payloads were flown or scheduled on POEM (PSLV Orbital Experimental Module) platforms.
Defining Roles and Responsibilities through the Indian Space Policy 2023
The
Indian Space Policy 2023
clearly defined the roles and responsibilities of key sectoral institutions. It established a framework for coordinated participation across the space sector.
Under the policy,
ISRO
would focus on advanced research, emerging technologies and national missions. Mature operational systems would be transferred to industry for manufacturing and commercial production.
The policy also formalised the respective roles of IN-SPACe and NSIL, as outlined in the
Cabinet Approval of Reforms section
. It reinforced IN-SPACe's role in promoting and authorising private-sector activities. It also strengthened NSIL's mandate to commercialise space technologies and services.
Additionally, the Indian Space Policy 2023 enabled private enterprises (NGEs) to undertake end-to-end space activities. These included satellite manufacturing, launch vehicle development and space-based services.
Liberalised FDI Policy for the Space Sector (February 2024)
For a long time, FDI was permitted in establishment and operation of satellites through the Government approval route only. Opening up this route was among the major policy reforms undertaken to boost private participation in the space sector. The Union Cabinet approved amendments to the Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy for the space sector
on 21 February 2024.
The revised provisions came into
effect on 16 April 2024
, allowing foreign investment through the automatic route within prescribed limits.
Under the automatic route, foreign investment is permitted up to 74% in satellite manufacturing and operation, satellite data products, and ground and user segments.
The limit is up to 49% in launch vehicles and spaceports, and up to 100% in components and subsystems.
Investment above the prescribed limits required Government approval.
Norms, Guidelines and Procedures (NGP) for Authorisation of Space Activities (May 2024)
IN-SPACe released the Norms, Guidelines and Procedures (NGP) on 3 May 2024 to put the Indian Space Policy 2023 into practice. The NGP explains which space activities need IN-SPACe authorisation, the criteria for granting it and the conditions applicants must follow. Any entity carrying out space activities to or from Indian territory, or within India’s jurisdiction, needs this authorisation.
Capital for Every Stage: IN-SPACe’s Funding Schemes for Space Start-ups
Pre-incubation Entrepreneurship (PIE)
- Launched in 2024, Pre-incubation Entrepreneurship (PIE) Programme is a 21-month programme with three phases:
ideation, innovation and prototype demonstration
. It is aimed at early-stage start-ups helping them to transform the idea into a prototype along with the development of entrepreneurs and allied business skills.
IN-SPACe Seed Fund Scheme
- Launched in 2023, the seed-fund scheme supports early-stage space start-ups (startups established on or after July 1, 2022). This scheme enables these start-ups to demonstrate the novel idea and graduate to next level. A maximum
grant of
₹
1 Crore
is provided to selected start-up on milestone basis in three or more instalments.
Technology Adoption Fund (TAF
) -
Once an idea works, the next challenge is turning it into a product. As part of this endeavor, the Technology Adoption Fund (TAF) was established in February 2025 with a
total outlay of ₹500 crore
. It promotes innovation and commercialisation of advanced technologies in the space sector. The fund provides partial financial support to Non-Government Entities (NGEs). It helps transform early-stage technologies into commercially viable products. Startups and MSMEs can receive up to 60% of the project cost. Moreover, large industries can receive up to 40%. However,
the funding is capped at ₹25 crore per project
.
Venture Capital Fund -
As start-ups grow, they need larger funds to expand. In 2024, the Union Cabinet approved setting up
of ₹1000 crore Venture Capital Fund
under aegis of IN-SPACe. The fund proposes an indicative investment range of ₹10–60 crore per company, depending on its stage of growth, growth trajectory and potential impact on national space capabilities. Equity investment is indicated at ₹10–30 crore for growth-stage companies and ₹30–60 crore for late growth-stage companies.
Key Outcomes from Marketisation of the Space Sector
Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-S
The reforms have opened launch activity to private enterprises, and each outcome reflects the results of this shift. The first major milestone of this expanded participation followed in November 2022. The Hyderabad-based
Skyroot Aerospace
successfully launched
Vikram-S
, India's
first privately developed rocket and the country's first private launch authorised by IN-SPACe
. Vikram-S, launched
under Mission Prarambh
, carried three customer payloads equipped with sensors to validate critical launch technologies for future orbital missions.
Agnikul Cosmos
In May 2024, Agnikul Cosmos became the first Non-Government Entity (NGE) to
launch a rocket from India’s first private launch pad
, Dhanush, at Sriharikota. The mission also demonstrated the world’s
first single-piece 3D-printed semi-cryogenic rocket engine
, showcasing advances in indigenous rocket manufacturing and propulsion technology
.
Click to Read More on Cryogenic Technology;
Click to Read More on 3D- Printing Tech
Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-I
On 18 July 2026, Skyroot Aerospace’s
small satellite launch vehicle Vikram-I
successfully reached orbit on its first flight. Known as Mission Aagaman, it was the
first time an Indian private company undertook an orbital launch of a rocket
from Indian soil, an outcome made possible by private participation under the space reforms.
Read More on Vikram-1
PSLV and SSLV: ISRO’s Launch Vehicles Now Built by Industry
The move to industry-led production is a landmark outcome of the space reforms. For decades, ISRO led the design and development of India’s launch vehicles, while Indian industry supplied components and services. The space-sector reforms have now opened the way for end-to-end industrial production.
On 5 September 2022, NSIL signed a contract with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL),
lead member of the HAL–L&T consortium, for the
production of five PSLV-XL (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle)
.
Additionally, on
10 September 2025, NSIL, ISRO, IN-SPACe and HAL signed the SSLV
(Small Satellite Launch Vehicle)
Technology Transfer Agreement, transferring SSLV technology to HAL
for industrial production. This led to the strengthening domestic manufacturing, widening industry participation and deepening public–private partnership.
India’s Space Sector on the Path to Viksit Bharat 2047
India’s space journey shows how clear policy, institutional trust and enterprising youth can turn ambition into achievement. With industry-led participation, the
Government projects the space economy to grow to about US$44 billion by 2033, around 8% of the global space economy
, and to
US$100 billion by 2040
. On the road to Viksit Bharat 2047, start-ups and MSMEs will work with ISRO, NSIL and IN-SPACe to build new capabilities, create skilled jobs and develop young talent. With sustained collaboration and skill development, this partnership reflects the spirit of Aatmanirbhar Bharat, Make in India and Start-up India.

title: Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum
subtitle: Preserving India’s Civilisational Heritage for Future Generations
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 NOV 2026 10:23AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Yuge Yugeen Bharat: A Museum for the Ages
India's civilisational heritage, spanning over 5,000 years, reflects a rich legacy of art, architecture, knowledge systems, traditions and cultural practices that have evolved over centuries. To preserve and present this heritage, the
Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum
is being developed as a landmark national cultural institution at the historic
North and South Block Complex in New Delhi
. Envisaged as a museum of the people, it will showcase the continuity, diversity and richness of India's civilisational journey through an integrated presentation of its tangible and intangible cultural heritage.
First announced by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on
18 May 2023
, the project received approval from the
Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs on 11 November 2026
, with an estimated total project cost of
₹
3,230 crore
. Being developed by the Ministry of Culture, the museum will transform the historic North and South Blocks, formerly housing key government offices, into public cultural spaces through adaptive reuse while preserving their architectural character. Planned as a museum of global scale, it will bring together historical collections, thematic galleries and modern exhibition technologies to make India's cultural heritage accessible to citizens, researchers and visitors from across the world.
From Historic Buildings to a World-Class Museum
The Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum will transform the historic
North and South Blocks
in New Delhi from centres of governance into public cultural spaces. Developed through
adaptive reuse
, the project will preserve the architectural heritage of these landmark buildings while creating modern exhibition spaces and visitor facilities. The museum is envisaged as a major cultural destination, combining heritage conservation with contemporary museum infrastructure.
Preserving Heritage Through Adaptive Reuse
Historic Significance:
The North and South Blocks served as centres of government administration until 13 February 2026, nearly 95 years after the inauguration of South Block. The South Block housed the Prime Minister's Office since Independence, and Cabinet meetings under 16 Prime Ministers were held in these buildings.
Transformation into Public Spaces:
Following the relocation of government offices to Seva Teerth, the new Prime Minister's Office, and the Kartavya Bhavans, the two buildings are being repurposed as part of the Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum.
Architectural Conservation:
The project will preserve the buildings' historic character, façades and architectural integrity through minimal intervention.
Reimagining Existing Spaces:
Courtyards, corridors and rooms will be adapted into galleries and exhibition areas, creating a unified museum experience.
Sustainable and Inclusive Design:
The redevelopment will prioritise sustainable resource use and universal accessibility.
A Museum of Global Scale
The proposed museum will rank among the world's largest cultural institutions in terms of exhibition space, with infrastructure designed to accommodate a substantial number of visitors.
Proposed Built-up Area:
Approximately
1,78,509 square metres
across the North and South Block Complex.
World's Largest Display Area:
The museum plans to offer more than
1 lakh square metres
of display space. This would exceed the display areas of the Louvre (73,000 sq. m), the British Museum (70,000 sq. m) and the Hermitage (66,800 sq. m).
Visitor Capacity:
Designed to accommodate
30,000 visitors
per day
and 1 crore
visitors annually.
Visitor Management:
Timed entry and crowd management systems are planned to facilitate convenient movement through the museum.
Public Amenities:
Proposed facilities include children's zones, food courts, souvenir shops and performance spaces, alongside accessible public areas.
The museum's development will thus combine the conservation of two historically significant buildings with the creation of a large-scale, accessible cultural institution for citizens and visitors from India and abroad.
Bringing India's Civilisational Journey to Life
The Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum will present India's civilisational journey through curated thematic galleries, historical collections and immersive experiences.
Phased Development and Implementation
The museum will be developed in phases, allowing galleries and exhibitions to be introduced progressively.
Implementation Period: FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31
.
First Gallery
: The
Adornment gallery
is expected to open to the public in the North Block in the later part of 2027.
Expansion of Galleries
: A modular approach is being formulated to add further thematic galleries in subsequent phases.
Project Oversight
: Implementation will involve coordinated project management, design and technical oversight, quality assurance and periodic monitoring.
The museum is expected to strengthen the preservation and public presentation of India's cultural heritage while creating opportunities for education, research, cultural engagement and tourism.
Thematic Galleries and Exhibitions
The museum will feature galleries on themes such as Architecture and Cityscapes, Mathematics and Astronomy, Languages and Scripts, Faith and Spirituality, and Bharat Connects - Trade and Ideas, among others.
These are among the themes identified for the museum, with additional galleries planned through a modular approach.
A Collection Reflecting India's Cultural Diversity
Approximately
18 lakh
objects have been identified for potential display at the museum, bringing together collections from different institutions across the country.
The identified objects are drawn from the
National Museum
, other museums under the Ministry of Culture,
52 Archaeological Survey of India
(ASI) site museums, various State museums and private collections.
Content and collection analysis is underway to determine how these objects will be incorporated into the museum's exhibitions.
The project also includes dedicated collection storage and conservation facilities to support the preservation and management of heritage objects.
Technology and Interactive Experiences
The museum will integrate contemporary technologies to make its exhibitions more engaging and accessible.
Immersive Experiences
: Planned use of
Augmented Reality (AR),
Virtual Reality (VR)
and
Artificial Intelligence (AI)
to support interactive interpretation and storytelling.
Digital Documentation
: The Ministry of Culture's collaboration with
Google Arts & Culture
, announced on 5 November 2026, includes digitisation efforts relating to the museum's historic buildings and collections.
Modern Museum Infrastructure
: Integration of intelligent building systems, exhibition technologies and conservation facilities to support museum operations and visitor experiences.
A Cultural Institution for Generations to Come
Beyond preserving and showcasing India's civilisational heritage, the
Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum
is expected to contribute to cultural tourism, education and research while creating opportunities for public engagement. As a national cultural institution, it will benefit a wide range of visitors, including
students, researchers, scholars, cultural practitioners, the general public, and domestic and international tourists
, offering opportunities to explore and appreciate India's diverse cultural legacy.
The project is expected to generate direct and indirect employment during its construction and operational phases. It is expected to create opportunities for artisans, craftspeople, researchers, museologists, designers, performers and other creative professionals, and to support livelihoods in the hospitality and tourism sectors. To promote Make in India, the project will encourage domestic manufacture of world-class museum materials and products through structured vendor development, creating opportunities for Indian artisans, manufacturers, conservation professionals and technology providers.
The museum is also expected to
generate recurring revenue
through ticket sales, food and beverage facilities, events and venue rentals, digital experiences, guided tours, retail outlets and other visitor services. With infrastructure planned to accommodate
up to 1 crore visitors annually
, the project aims to combine long-term cultural preservation with public accessibility and revenue-generating visitor services. Its educational, cultural and tourism-related benefits are intended to extend to visitors from across India and abroad.

content:
Adi Vaani
is an AI-powered platform of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs that makes tribal languages more accessible through translation and digital tools. As on 15 October 2026, it supports text translation in
nine tribal languages
and has recorded
over 35,000
Android downloads. State Tribal Research Institutes have contributed approximately
13.9 lakh
text sentences and around
300 hours
of speech data to train its models. The Working Group on Tribal Languages, which first met on 15 October 2026, discussed positioning Adi Vaani as the National Tribal Language Repository. By reducing language barriers, it can support mother-tongue education, healthcare communication, access to public services and cultural preservation.
Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs is observing
Janjatiya Gaurav Pakhwada
across the country from
1 to 15 November 2026
, culminating in
Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas on 15 November
, the birth anniversary of
Dharti Aaba Bhagwan Birsa Munda
. The Government of India designated 15 November as Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas in
2021
. The Pakhwada is a focused, time-bound drive to accelerate the Ministry’s flagship programmes and take their benefits to tribal families at the last mile. On Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas,
over 300 projects
for tribal communities across States are being taken up, with
228 ready for inauguration
and
74 for foundation stone laying
. Two national digital initiatives, the
Jan-HIT Portal
and the
National FRA Digital Platform
, are also being launched. Tribal Research Institutes have planned
more than 160 activities in 19 States/UTs
.

A language is more than a means of communication. It carries the history, identity and knowledge of a community.
Across India, tribal languages have carried folk tales, songs and valuable knowledge of forests, farming and medicine across generations. Yet many are
low-resource languages
, spoken by relatively small communities and passed down largely through oral traditions. With limited written records and very little digital text or speech data, these languages have remained largely unsupported by modern language technologies.
Adi Vaani aims to bridge this gap by using artificial intelligence. It uses technology to document, translate and promote tribal languages
, creating new opportunities for their preservation, learning and everyday use.
Adi Vaani: Connecting Language with Technology
Adi Vaani
is an AI-powered translation and language platform built with tribal communities, for tribal communities. Launched by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs on
1 September 2025
, it was developed by a national consortium led by
IIT Delhi
, along with BITS Pilani, IIIT Hyderabad, IIIT Nava Raipur and the Tribal Research Institutes (TRIs) of Jharkhand, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Meghalaya. Over time, several other State Tribal Research Institutes (TRIs) also joined the initiative, further expanding its collaborative reach across the country.
Bridging the Digital Divide: Mission and Vision
Adi Vaani aims to bridge the digital divide for tribal communities through AI-powered translation. Its vision is a digitally inclusive India where no citizen is left behind due to language barriers. The initiative is guided by respect, collaboration, authenticity, innovation and empowerment through digital inclusion.
Expanding Language Coverage and Digital Reach
Starting with
Santali, Bhili, Mundari and Gondi
, Adi Vaani has expanded to offer
text translation in nine tribal languages
as on 15 October 2026. It also provides speech translation, Optical Character Recognition (OCR), video subtitling and access to more than
300 language primers
. Primers are basic language learning resources designed to help new learners understand and practise tribal languages easily. The platform has recorded
over 35,000 Android downloads and around 6,500 monthly users
, indicating its growing digital reach.
Building AI with Tribal Communities
What makes Adi Vaani different is its
community-based approach
. Native speakers contribute words, sentences and voice recordings through TRIs and AdiKosh. These are checked by language experts before being used to train AI models. The project aims to collect around
1,00,000 sentence pairs and 100 hours of speech recordings per language
. As on 15 October 2026, State TRIs had contributed approximately
13.9 lakh text sentences across ten languages and around 300 hours of speech data.
This approach combines modern technology with community knowledge to support the preservation, learning and everyday use of tribal languages. Each language passes through five phases, from data collection to integration on the platform, and the models are retrained as the community contributes more data.
What Are TRIs and AdiKosh?
Tribal Research Institutes (TRIs)
are research bodies established at the State level under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs. They serve as centres of knowledge and research, functioning as think tanks for tribal development. TRIs preserve tribal cultural heritage, while providing research-based inputs to States for evidence-based planning and appropriate legislation. They build the capacity of tribal communities, as well as of individuals and institutions associated with tribal affairs. They also disseminate information and create awareness on tribal issues.
AdiKosh is the word bank of Adi Vaani. It holds dictionary entries and spoken sentences, recorded by verified speakers and reviewed by the language team. Speech recorded through AdiKosh is validated by TRIs before it is used to train the models.
The platform’s key features include:
Text-to-text translation:
Translation between supported tribal languages and languages such as Hindi and English.
Speech-to-text:
Converts spoken words into text, supporting oral-language documentation.
Speech-to-speech translation:
Translates speech by linking speech recognition, translation and speech synthesis.
Optical Character Recognition (OCR):
Extracts text from images and scanned documents for translation.
Video subtitling:
Supports translation of video content and public information into tribal languages.
Digital dictionaries and primers:
Provide vocabulary, meanings and basic learning resources.
Tribal Languages: Preserving Knowledge and Identity
According to
Census 2011
, India has
about 10.45 crore Scheduled Tribe people
, accounting for about
8.6% of the country’s population
. These communities have distinct languages and cultural traditions. Preserving these languages is important as they carry centuries of folklore, traditional knowledge and community identity. They also support early learning in the mother tongue and help pass knowledge of forests, farming, medicine and biodiversity to future generations. Making these languages digitally accessible can further reduce language barriers and improve access to education, healthcare information and public services.
